result.summary: Adds a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow that runs weekly to inspect the Windows code signing certificate. If the certificate is within 90 days of expiry or already expired, the workflow automatically files a GitHub issue with the certificate details and relevant commit. It suppresses duplicate issues by checking for existing closed or open reports matching the target expiration date.
result.problem: There is no automated check for code signing certificate expiration. Maintainers currently notice expired certificates during release candidate builds, which risks delaying urgent or short-notice bugfix releases while waiting for renewals.
evidence: Author notes: "Currently we have no automation in place to check that our code signing certificates are not expired or close to expiry. We have previously 'relied on Release Candidates' as a dry-run for codesigners to realise that a certificate has expired and have time to fix it. 'Noticing during RC cycle' also might not be appropriate in the future if we release more bugfix minor/patch releases on short notice."
result.changed_since_previous: The implementation is now provided in a GitHub Actions workflow that checks the repository's PEM bundle with OpenSSL and uses the GitHub CLI to detect duplicate issues before filing.
result.card: Adds a weekly GitHub Actions workflow to check the Windows code signing certificate and open an issue if it expires within 90 days. Bitcoin Core currently has no automated monitoring for certificate expiration, relying on release candidate cycles for codesigners to discover expired certificates. The author notes that relying on regular release cycles is prone to delaying urgent, short-notice bugfix releases.

risk.why: The workflow only runs on a schedule in GitHub Actions to check certificate dates and cannot affect release binaries or node runtime behavior.
